newsitem.title: USA: Talks start between Columbia, feds on investigation.
newsitem.headline: Talks start between Columbia, feds on investigation.

text.p: Talks have begun between lawyers for Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. and federal investigators as the company deals with a massive probe into its business practices, President and Chief Operating Officer Jack Bovender said on Wednesday.
Separately, the Florida attorney general's office said it several months ago launched its own probe into the giant health care company, joining Alabama and Texas in such a move.

Appointed on Monday as second-in-command at the embattled company, Bovender told Reuters in an interview that he has not scheduled a meeting with federal authorities, but a formal dialogue involving top executives may come soon.

"I think our lawyers are talking to them. The initial meetings can occur, I think, fairly quickly. But exactly how the dialogue and definitive discussions are going to go, I am not sure. The lawyers have that with them right now," he said.

A new team is taking over at the largest U.S. for-profit hospital firm amid a storm of controversy that saw the ouster two weeks ago of former top executives, the indictments of three middle managers last week on fraud charges, the filing of 11 shareholder lawsuits and other troubles.

Bovender was named as a key lieutenant to Dr. Thomas Frist, who was appointed chief executive and chairman on July 24. Bovender said his early internal discussions have revealed a need for deep changes within Columbia, not only in certain business practices, but in overall style.

He spoke at length about values, as Frist has done, and stressed that he does not see a new management style holding back Columbia's historically robust growth, a worry that some Wall Street analysts have expressed in recent days.
"The things I have seen call for systemic changes in some practices to make sure that we don't create errors or that we don't create the appearance of improprieties," Bovender said.

"The management style we're talking about is totally compatible with growth. In fact, I think over the long haul, it is the way that you promote and get sustainable growth ... I don't know where we got in this country the idea that the only way you can grow companies is by running over everybody to do it," he said.
Stomping the competition was a Columbia hallmark under ousted former Chairman and CEO Richard Scott, analysts said.

A lawyer by training, Scott assembled the $20-billion company over just 10 years by gobbling up rivals and applying a rigorous bottom-line calculus to a business that likes to see itself as concerned with more than making money.
It remains uncertain whether Scott's method of challenging managers with ambitious financial targets caused some to push, knowingly or not, the legal and ethical limits, Bovender said.
"The things I have seen so far would not indicate to me wilful actions," he said. "But again, bear with me. This is a two-day assessment and there are a lot of things to be done."

Federal agents have seized cartloads of internal Columbia files in a probe focused on home health care, laboratory billing and other activities. The new managers at the company are focusing on the same areas, Bovender said.
"Those are areas that we're putting a lot of time into and will have teams working on," he said.
In response to a question, Bovender that added he viewed as possible an extension of Columbia's stock buyback programme.

"That's possible and I think there are probably other combinations and permutations that are possible going forward in the next few months .... Exactly what that will look like, whether it will be more buybacks or other kinds of initiatives that increase shareholder value, I don't know," he said.
Columbia shares rose 50 cents to $34.25 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon, extending a slight rebound this week following two weeks of sharp declines.
